fullText:
AUSTIN, Texas (AP) — A U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer shot and wounded a man Sunday afternoon in Austin, Texas, local authorities said, and anti-ICE protesters quickly gathered at the scene.

The man was in serious but stable condition at a hospital after being shot once in the torso on the capital city's north side, Austin officials said at a news conference.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, did not participate in the news conference and didn't respond to repeated requests for details.

City police officers were not involved in the operation or the shooting, which occurred after a traffic stop, Austin Police Chief Lisa Davis said while briefing reporters along with the city's mayor and other officials.

Mayor Kirk Watson, a Democrat, said he wants the city's police department to have a role in the investigation so it can provide "clear, third-party eyes" in the process. Watson said he does not think it would be appropriate for ICE to conduct an investigation on its own.

Austin residents have "a right to feel safe in their city," Watson said. A proper investigation will only enhance credibility, he added.

The chief said there were not many facts she could provide so soon after the incident but added that her department's special investigation unit was at the scene.

The Texas Department of Public Safety said it received a request from ICE for assistance in a vehicle pursuit around 12:50 p.m. By the time DPS troopers arrived, the shooting had already taken place, the department said in a statement Sunday evening.

An immigration attorney representing the man's family identified him as Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, a 28-year-old Venezuelan man.

Attorney Kate Lincoln Goldfinch said in a video posted to her Instagram account that she believed he had no criminal history and no final order of removal from the U.S., but she later told The Associated Press that she did not know his current immigration status.

The man's family has struggled to get any information from the hospital about his status or location, Lincoln-Goldfinch said.

Just before 7 p.m., the man's wife was informed by the hospital's attorney that the man had been released into ICE custody a few hours earlier, Lincoln-Goldfinch wrote in a text to AP.

"No one bothered to update her," she wrote.

It wasn't immediately clear if the man remained hospitalized while in ICE custody or if he had been transferred elsewhere.

A dark blue Toyota Corolla was parked under an overpass with damage to its passenger-side door and what appeared to be bullet holes. The car was towed away in the early evening and traffic began moving again.

A large law enforcement presence was present along with a crowd of about a hundred protesters. Some demonstrators cursed at police officers holding riot shields, while others yelled out as passing cars honked in support of the protest. One man held a sign saying, "Nobody is safe" and, on the other side, "ICE Nazi."

Asked if Austin authorities knew where the involved federal agent is, given that agents have left states after previous shootings nationwide, the mayor said: "We do not know that. But my hope would be that, an agent that's involved in an officer-involved shooting would not leave the city. Certainly not leave the state."

The office of Travis County District Attorney José Pompa Garza asked that local police and prosecutors be included in the investigation.

"We further request cooperation from the federal government in giving us access to the evidence," the DA's office said in a statement Sunday evening.

U.S. Rep. Greg Casar, a Democrat representing parts of Austin, called for transparency as the shooting is investigated.

"It is awful that this horror has come to our doorstep," Casar told reporters. "For Austin to be safe, ICE should end its surge here."

The shooting comes as ICE surges enforcement across the country this summer, producing more than 50,000 arrests a month for the first time in its history in July and August.

In July, an ICE officer fatally shot 52-year-old Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, of Houston, after federal agents driving unmarked vehicles pursued him while he was taking his construction crew to a job site.

Also in July, 25-year-old Johan Sebastián, a Colombian man, was shot by an ICE officer in Maine. The officer is an Army veteran who has struggled with serious mental health issues since early childhood and never should have been given a badge and gun to patrol American streets, several of his close relatives told AP.

The administration's enforcement efforts were widely condemned last winter after the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good in Minnesota.

Weber reported from Los Angeles and Boone from Boise, Idaho. Contributing were Associated Press journalists Kimberlee Kruesi in Providence, Rhode Island and Tim Sullivan in Minneapolis.

title: 'He died in my arms': Patrick Clancy opens up about the grief of losing 3 children
description:
Patrick Clancy said he felt he had no purpose after his three children were killed.
"There was a time where I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday," Clancy, 36, said in an interview with 60 Minutes. "And I was completely fine with it."
His interview with correspondent Ross Douthat comes after his ex-wife's mistrial earlier this month. The court has yet to determine whether Patrick's ex-wife, Lindsay Clancy, will be retried for the killings of their children: 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan.
fullText:
Patrick Clancy said he felt he had no purpose after his three children were killed.

"There was a time where I didn't think I would live to see my 35th birthday," Clancy, 36, said in an interview with 60 Minutes. "And I was completely fine with it."

His interview with correspondent Ross Douthat comes after his ex-wife's mistrial earlier this month. The court has yet to determine whether Patrick's ex-wife, Lindsay Clancy, will be retried for the killings of their children: 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. It also comes as Patrick and his wife, Rachel Danis, face intense public scrutiny, becoming the subjects of online suspicion and speculation on social media.

In October 2022, five months after Callan's birth, Patrick said Lindsay told him she had gone a few nights without sleeping.

Over the next two months, Lindsay made repeated emergency room visits. She admitted herself to a program for patients with postpartum depression and was discharged after a day of treatment. Lindsay was also prescribed an escalating number of prescription drugs.

Patrick said he struggled to help his wife navigate the medical system and did not know how to manage a postpartum illness.

"I think mental illness has this ability to be tragically deceptive," he said.

December was the low point, Patrick said. "It was a big struggle for her — just a huge lack of sleep, deep, deep depression, intrusive thoughts."

Lindsay checked herself into McLean Psychiatric Hospital on New Year's Eve. She was treated for depression and released days later, making it home in time to celebrate Cora's birthday on Jan. 7.

Less than three weeks later, Patrick said he came home from an errand to find Lindsay lying in the backyard, her throat and wrists cut, paralyzed after jumping from an upstairs window.

He said he found his children strangled in the basement. Cora and Dawson were dead. Callan was airlifted to Boston Children's Hospital.

"I really thought there was a chance that Callan would live," Patrick recalled. "I remember just thinking, 'Just give me one. Just give me one kid, and I would raise him as best I could, and I would give him the best life I possibly could. I'd tell him about his brother and sister.' And I was holding out hope for that."

Callan's heart kept beating for four days.

"I got to hold him. I got to lay down next to him. And he died in my arms," Patrick said.

Patrick Clancy forgives his ex-wife

In the days after the tragedy, Patrick wrote tributes to each of his three children and decided to publicly forgive Lindsay.

"I saw headlines that said, you know, 'Killer Mom,' and 'Baby Murderer,' 'Monster.' And none of them were accurate," Patrick said. "I think if people said, 'She did a horrible thing,' I think everyone could agree with that. …But I believe that it was her mental illness that caused that." So I shared those words."

Lindsay never asked for forgiveness, but Patrick said he gave it to her. They've both brought medical malpractice lawsuits against health care providers who treated Lindsay. Some have denied wrongdoing, and others have yet to respond to the claim.

Patrick said he thinks he "did the best I could with what I had at the time. And I live with the outcome. I live with it every day."

Patrick said he realized he could no longer stay in Duxbury and moved to New York City that April, seeking anonymity.

Trial in court — and in the court of public opinion

In July, Lindsay Clancy's trial began. Her lawyers argued she was suffering from dangerous postpartum psychosis and couldn't be held criminally responsible for her actions.

The trial became a national obsession – generating furious arguments about the relationship between mental illness and criminal fault, how the medical system fails mothers and how men and women understand one another.

Patrick testified and found himself at the center of an online swarm of sleuths and influencers dissecting every detail of the case, developing theories that portray him as uncaring, unfaithful and even the murderer of his children.

"It's painful to see. And it makes it difficult to be in public and it's possible that some of those people, after seeing lie after lie after lie, they start to believe it and that's what we're left with," he said.

One of the catalysts for the theories about Patrick was his apparent stoicism on the witness stand. Patrick said that testifying was difficult for him and that he had a "massive, traumatic" panic attack on the second day of his testimony.

"They put me in an ambulance," Patrick said. "They offered me some medication, but I said, 'I don't want it, because I want to go back and I want to finish this so I can be done with this.' And I went back and I finished the testimony."

Lindsay's trial ended with a hung jury earlier this month.

Patrick says reaching out to survivors and experts in the field of postpartum health has helped him move forward. He remarried this April to Dr. Rachel Danis, a fertility doctor in New York City.

Danis said the pair met in January 2024 in a New York City run club and got to know each other over coffee.

"Pat pulled out his phone to pay, and I noticed this adorable photo of children as the wallpaper," Danis said. " I just asked, 'Who are those cuties?' And Pat said, 'Those are my kids.' And then I think I asked if they live in Massachusetts, and Pat said, 'They died.' And this is just at the cashier."

Danis said she tried to "take some of the weight from Pat."

"I can't bring his kids back," she said. "But if I can honor them and allow Pat to grieve but also just continue to honor them in the present, it, I guess that's all I can do."

The pair are starting a family, and Patrick is preparing to one day tell his future child about their older siblings, Cora, Dawson and Callan.

"I think every parent can agree, you have different relationships with your kids, but they're all your kids," he said. "And I can't wait to tell them about their brothers and sister."

title: Yu, 13, wins record-breaking first major gold medal
description: China’s Yu Zidi, 13, wins a record‑breaking 200m women’s butterfly gold at the Asian Games in Tokyo.
fullText:
Chinese schoolgirl Yu Zidi lit up the opening day of the Asian Games with a record‑breaking 200m butterfly gold medal secured by a performance she described as "only so‑so".

The 13‑year‑old claimed her first major gold in two minutes 05.08 seconds, an Asian Games record that took almost half a second off compatriot Zhang Yufei's mark from three years ago.

Yu, who is strongly tipped to make an impact at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics, won by over three seconds in Tokyo from her team-mate Chang Mohan.

"It was only so-so," a smiling Yu said after receiving her medal, adding that her butterfly technique "is still slightly lacking".

"I hope I can swim even faster. I improved my time by 0.9 seconds here, and I believe I will perform better next time," she continued.

Yu, who will take part in two more individual events at the Asian Games, became the youngest ever swimmer to win a medal at the World Championships when she took bronze as a 12-year-old as part of China's 4x200m freestyle relay team last year.

title: Neville calls Man Utd 'pathetic' - but Carrick maintains belief
description: Gary Neville calls Manchester United "pathetic", but boss Michael Carrick maintains belief after salvaging draw at Fulham.
fullText:
Gary Neville took a deep breath after Lisandro Martinez's own goal put Fulham ahead just over an hour into what had been a laboured Manchester United performance, and delivered his verdict.

The former United skipper is never short of a scathing word, but even by his standards, this was brutal.

"I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen," he said. "Absolutely pathetic.

"I've never seen such a lack of effort. What must [Michael] Carrick be thinking?"

For context, Neville was part of the United side beaten 3-1 by Sunday's opponents Fulham at Old Trafford in October 2003. In recent memory they have also lost 7-0 at Liverpool and 6-1 at home twice, to Tottenham and Manchester City.

Neville's words came after a poor quarter of an hour from the start of the second half to Martinez's moment of ill fortune, before United went on to snatch a 1-1 draw thanks to Matheus Cunha's deflected strike in the 89th minute.

It seemed an extreme reaction. But in a week when United lost the Manchester derby to a City side reduced to 10 men midway through the first half, then against Brighton for the first time in more than 50 years were beaten at home after giving away a two-goal lead, frustration among the fanbase is high.

Questions over fitness were first raised during pre-season when midfielder Youri Tielemans revealed United were not prioritising running.

While Cunha did not exactly agree with Neville in his post-match interview with Sky Sports, his comments will have fuelled more debate around the issue.

"At the beginning of the second half they put in more energy than us," said the Brazilian. "We cannot accept this."

Unsurprisingly, Carrick had a different take. He used the way his side tried to pressure the home team in the latter stages, leading to Cunha's equaliser, as evidence his squad is fit enough.

"The way we finished the game, actually, it didn't look like that. We finished the game really strong actually, and kept pushing. I don't think that's an issue, no," he said.

Cunha also mentioned the "noise" around United when he spoke to BBC Match of the Day.

Neville is a significant part of that noise, either directly or through his growing media empire.

Carrick has previously said he can shut it out.

It cannot be quite so easy though when United fans - who usually back their team through disappointment - followed up chants on Wednesday in disgust at the Brighton debacle by here booing Carrick's decision to take off popular England midfielder Kobbie Mainoo 11 minutes from time.

"There's always going to be certain reactions when you're making changes," said Carrick. "I've spoken to Kobbie after the game and he's absolutely fine.

"I understand at times when we are chasing the game, everyone's a little bit emotional. The supporters are, as well they should be, desperate for us to do the right thing.

"But I don't take any negatives or offence to it. I think we've just got to try and keep doing the right things to get back into the game.

"The supporters were unbelievable today, I have to say, all the way through, and stuck with the boys and supported them. At least we've given them something small at the end to take from it, and I'm sure there's more to come."

A draw at Fulham is "something small" considering the home side started the game at the foot of the Premier League - and have now swapped places with Tottenham.

Five points from five games leaves United 12th, an incredible 10 points behind pacesetters Manchester City already.

Their £70m summer signing Carlos Baleba is still to make his debut, and long-term injury victim Matthijs de Ligt was not involved at all, even though both were part of the squad that travelled south on Saturday.

Striker Benjamin Sesko also missed the game after suffering a recurrence of the shin problem against Brighton that he was troubled by for an extended period last season before submitting to a recovery programme that ruled him out for more than three months.

Carrick says "at this point" the extent of the damage is unknown.

This would all be pretty underwhelming were it not for the ticketing issues instigated by the club's touting crackdown that has annoyed so many in the fanbase.

On Wednesday, United will release their full-year financial results to 30 June, around which the full extent of their current debt will be revealed.

Then there is the general debate about the wisdom of new stadium, which is set to cost in excess of £2bn, with planning permission potentially submitted with the main Old Trafford masterplan, which is earmarked for late 2027 or early 2028.

Little wonder, after leading United back to the Champions League so unexpectedly last season, Carrick is presiding over a club whose supporters feel deflated, even if he does not recognise that.

"It's still a big season ahead," he said. "It's a long season and you're going to have spells through a season. That's part of the journey.

"It's not a sprint, it's a long effort.

"I'm not playing it down, you know. We wanted more points, so I'm not saying everything's great. I understand the frustration. We wanted to be better and we wanted to do other things.

"But deflation is certainly not what we have within the club and within the group. The players didn't have that on the pitch today and that's what will carry us through the season without a doubt."

title: Elvira loses nerve as Spaun triumphs at Wentworth
description: Manuel Elvira choked back the tears as an elated JJ Spaun celebrated becoming only the third US player to win the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth.
fullText:
BMW PGA Championship - final round

-17 JJ Spaun (US); -15 M Elvira (Spa), R McIlroy (NI), A Scott (Aus), A Rai (Eng)

Selected others:-14 M Fitzpatrick (Eng), R Fox (NZ); -13 R MacIntyre (Sco), M Wallace (Eng), A Sullivan (Eng); -12 A Noren (Swe), R Fisher (Eng); -11 S Lowry (Ire) A Fitzpatrick (Eng); -10 V Hovland (Nor), L Aberg (Swe), J Niemann (Chi), T Hatton (Eng)

Golf can be a cruel game. As Spain's Manuel Elvira choked back the tears on Sunday, just a short distance away an elated JJ Spaun celebrated becoming only the third player from the United States to win the BMW PGA Championship at Wentworth.

The 2025 US Open champion joins Billy Horschel and the legendary Arnold Palmer on a storied list of winners that also includes Tony Jacklin, Sir Nick Faldo, Seve Ballesteros, Jose Maria Olazabal and Rory McIlroy.

However, it was hard not to feel sympathy for Elvira, the unknown 30-year-old from Santander.

Ranked 294th in the world, this had looked like being the moment he had longed for when he stepped on to the final tee with a first victory in his sights - straight off the back of outrageous eagle on the 17th.

Having twice made birdies on the friendly par five this week, a third was hardly implausible - while a par would have ensured a play-off with Spaun, already in the clubhouse at 17 under par.

Instead Elvira, who opted for an iron off the tee, found a fairway bunker when he took the conservative option to lay up.

To compound matters he then missed the green with his approach, almost finding the grandstand, and duffed his fourth into the sand after being given a free drop.

Once he escaped he took a further two putts, and his double-bogey seven finish deprived him of even ending the tournament in outright second place.

"[It was] devastating that I hit the wrong shot at the right time on the lay up and left myself the toughest shot in the fairway bunker, and wasn't able to pull it off," Elvira said.

"I've played some of the best golf probably of my life."

While it was not at the level of Jean Van de Velde's implosion at the 1999 Open Championship or, more recently, Jordan Spieth's misadventures in the 2016 Masters - it nevertheless made for difficult viewing.

And his brother Ignacio - who had earlier finished in a tie for 44th - was left to console his younger sibling as they walked off the 18th green.

Speaking on BBC Radio 5 Live, former Europe Solheim Cup player Trish Johnson said: "It's a truly awful feeling. No more than 20 minutes ago he's got this huge dream.

"To watch that unfold on 18 was really, in golfing terms, quite tragic. What he has to remember is how he put himself in that position.

"In a big event like this the chances are we'll never see him in that position to win this calibre of tournament ever again, and that's very sad."

As Elvira trudged away after ending on 15 under alongside major champions McIlroy, Adam Scott and Aaron Rai, which in any other circumstances could have been considered a triumph, Spaun was already rejoicing his first title outside of the US.

While that will earn him a hefty pay cheque of about £1.1m, he said his omission from the US Presidents Cup - a tournament where America face a rest-of-the-world team, excluding Europe - had been the driving force behind his success.

Spaun outlined that he had been given the news in a 45-second phone call, in which he was told he was the "odd man out".

"I played with a huge chip on my shoulder. I definitely had something to prove this week but everything happens for a reason," said Spaun, who carded a five-under 67 on Sunday, crucially including four birdies in the concluding five holes.

"My whole career, I've kind of had to do that. I wasn't given scholarships. I had a walk-on. I had to earn my PGA Tour card the hard way. I was never given sponsor invite opportunities. I just had to do everything the hard way.

"Being left off the Presidents Cup team a couple weeks ago was very disappointing, and you know, I wanted to prove that I deserve to be on that team."

One amusing aspect of Spaun's round was seeing his wife Melody walking around the grounds of the famous Surrey club with a Jeremy Clarkson mask.

"We've grown fond of him - along with the English culture, we actually take holidays in December in the Cotswolds - and we really enjoy his show [Clarkson's Farm]," Spaun added.

"I went to his pub, with the hopes of catching a glimpse of him, but he wasn't around.

"My wife said we would have a surprise guest following me this week if I competed in the tournament and, sure enough, I see the face of Jeremy Clarkson and her holding it. Jeremy was there in spirit and I think he brought me good fortune."

While Spaun's putter ran hot, McIlroy made five birdies and a bogey on Sunday, in a round that also included four birdie misses from inside 10 feet.

The one consolation for the six-time major winner is that he made a huge dent in Patrick Reed's lead in the Race to Dubai standings as he goes for a record-equalling eighth title.

"I'm excited. I have three events until the end of my DP World Tour season. I'm not sure what Patrick's schedule looks like coming up, but I feel like I have enough opportunities," McIlroy said.

"I'm excited for the opportunity, and it would be obviously amazing to match Monty's record."

title: What have we learned from the Premier League so far?
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the opening weeks of the Premier League season as a long international break arrives.
fullText:
The Premier League takes a near three-week break as we enter a four-game international window.

So, what have we learned from the opening five matches of the season?

Premier League champions Arsenal were looking fairly unstoppable in the opening weeks of the season.

A win over Brighton on Saturday would have given the Gunners a club-record equalling eighth consecutive win in all competitions to start the season.

But that all ended with a 3-0 loss at Amex Stadium on Saturday.

The Gunners had not lost a league game by more than one goal, let alone three, since October 2024.

It was their heaviest defeat in the league since May 2023 when they lost 3-0 to the same opposition.

"That's not going to take away what the team has done and the boys have done in the last six or seven weeks since coming back from the World Cup," said boss Mikel Arteta.

"What we've done, the way we've competed and the amount of games we've won has been remarkable - but this is a big lesson for all of us to understand what it takes to win at this level."

Brighton humbling 'a big lesson' for Arsenal - Arteta

Many wondered if Manchester City would experience a post-Pep Guardiola slump when the legendary boss left after a decade.

Things did not start too well under Enzo Maresca, with the Community Shield defeat by Arsenal.

But they have won all five games in the Premier League - and seven in a row in all competitions - after Sunday's entertaining 5-3 win over Sunderland.

That takes them three points clear of Arsenal.

"In the press conference before the game, I said I expect a very tough game," said Maresca. "Then we also conceded two or three goals but we have learned a lot in these eight weeks and this is good."

Perfect 24 hours as Man City put pressure on Arsenal

Brighton and Brentford, two clubs who have never won a major trophy, have continued to impress this season.

Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton enjoyed that 3-0 win over Arsenal to see them sit third in the table, only two points behind the Gunners.

Brighton have won at home against the reigning Premier League champions in each of the last three seasons.

Star player Pascal Gross laughed and said "no" when BBC Sport asked him if Albion were in the title race.

But stranger things have happened...

Meanwhile, just one point below them in the table are Keith Andrews' Brentford.

Many tipped the Bees to struggle after the departure of Thomas Frank last summer but if anything they improved under their former set-piece coach Andrews.

And their start to this season - unbeaten after five games and fourth in the table - is showing he is no one-season wonder as a manager.

They go into the break on the back of their most impressive result, a 3-0 home win over Chelsea.

Leeds, impressing again under boss Daniel Farke, are also on nine points and in a potential Champions League place.

Andoni Iraola's Liverpool and Everton are just below them on goal difference.

From near oblivion to Europe - Brighton celebrate 125th anniversary in style

Seven years apart, United did the same thing twice hoping for different results - appointing a club legend who last managed in Britain in the Championship after a good start as caretaker boss.

In 2019 it was Ole Gunnar Solskjaer and this time it was Michael Carrick.

But this season, after Carrick having a summer to work on his team, the Red Devils have only won once in the league.

Their five points after five league games is their joint fewest at this stage of a Premier League season.

They go into the international break on the back of a 1-1 draw against Fulham, and even needed a late deflected Matheus Cunha strike to stop the Cottagers winning their first game all season.

After the Lisandro Martinez own goal that give Fulham the lead, ex-United captain Gary Neville said on Sky Sports: "I've watched Manchester United since the age of five and that's the worst 15 minutes I've ever seen.

"Absolutely pathetic. I've never seen such a lack of effort."

United's owners will have almost three weeks to stew on this before they host fellow underachievers Tottenham (more on them soon) on 10 October.

In 2024 and 2025, the three promoted teams went straight back down - mostly with really low points tallies too.

But that streak came to an end last year when Sunderland finished seventh to qualify for Europe and Leeds came 14th. Only Burnley went down.

And the early weeks of this season indicate we could be in for a similar situation.

Hull City are eighth after five games, with their 2-1 loss to Newcastle their first defeat.

Ipswich are 11th. And Coventry, after losing the first four games without scoring, beat Nottingham Forest 1-0 and only sit in the drop zone on goal difference.

A Coventry win 25 years in the making

Tottenham finished 17th the last two seasons, their lowest two finishes since being in the second tier in 1977-78.

But expectations were raised after a summer of big spending - with Spurs splashing out £302m as well as making two high-profile loan signings.

Defence and midfield in particular were overhauled, with new wingers too.

But they are left with one senior striker in Dominic Solanke, who has only scored 12 Premier League goals in over two years at the club.

"I feel they have overpaid for every player they bought this summer - you can't rule them out from being in and around the relegation battle," said TNT pundit and ex-England international Joe Cole.

Saturday's 3-2 loss against Aston Villa sees them sit 19th going into the break - despite scoring their first two league goals of the campaign.

"We have to put on the pitch something more than we are putting," said manager Roberto de Zerbi.

"Football is tactical but it is blood, it is fighting, it is first one on the ball. We will suffer until the next game."

No revival in sight for 'fragile' Spurs after Villa defeat

Many were keen to see what Xabi Alonso could do at Chelsea this season.

The Spaniard memorably led Bayer Leverkusen to a historic unbeaten German double in 2023-24.

And they made big changes to their squad this summer, with £117m attacking midfielder Morgan Rogers and new first-choice keeper Emiliano Martinez both coming in from Aston Villa.

There have been 22 goals in their five league games - more coming against them than for them - and they sit 10th.

And that is not even counting the 6-3 win over Leeds in the Carabao Cup.

Hugely entertaining for the neutrals - but perhaps not for Chelsea fans or management.
